title: Mary Magdalene (22 July)
hookLine: the apostle to the apostles now has a full feast day

lines: A PICTURE THE GOSPELS DON'T PAINT.
cards: Long loose hair, a jar of ointment at her elbow, eyes lifted, sometimes a skull on the table beside her. In some old paintings, that woman is Mary Magdalene, the weeping sinner. But the Gospels don't paint that picture.
They never call her a prostitute. What they give her is something else entirely: a job. She's sent with a message, and the people she carries it to are the apostles themselves.
That's why one of her old titles sounds like a riddle: the apostle to the apostles. Today, Mary Magdalene.

teach.h: HEALED, NOT A SINNER IN THE TEXT.
teach.b: Luke introduces her among the women traveling with Jesus: "Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils."
Healed, then: not a sinner in the text, someone set free. These women "ministered unto him of their substance": they paid for the mission out of their own money. John places her at the cross.
And on Easter morning, in John's Gospel, she's alone at the tomb, crying, until the risen Jesus calls her by name and she knows him. Then the part that's easy to skip. He doesn't let her hold on.
He gives her an errand: "go to my brethren, and say unto them, I ascend unto my Father, and your Father; and to my God, and your God." And she goes.
"Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the LORD, and that he had spoken these things unto her." In John, she tells them before Jesus appears to the others that evening.

So where did the sinner come from? Over time, some Western preaching merged her with other women in the Gospels: the unnamed woman who weeps on Jesus's feet in Luke, and Mary of Bethany. The texts never join them.
Orthodox Christians, who didn't take up that merging, honor her as equal to the apostles.

The Catholic Church now keeps her day as a full feast, and uses that old title: apostle to the apostles. Different churches, one thing in common. The first words of Easter, in John, travel through her.

how: On Mary Magdalene's day, churches that keep it read John 20's garden scene; the Catholic Church keeps it as a feast, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles.

that you have seen the Lord, and what he said to you.

games.why: "Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the LORD, and that he had spoken these things unto her."

practice: Bring to mind a woman who told you something true that changed things, a grandmother, a teacher, a nurse, a stranger on a bad day, maybe someone who wasn't believed at first, and remember what she said and how she said it.
If you pray, thank God for her by name, the way the church remembers Mary Magdalene by name; if you don't, thank her in your mind, and let her words be heard properly this time.

wordCard.voice: Mary Magdalene. Healed and sent, the woman at the tomb who carried the news of Easter to the apostles, remembered with a feast of her own.

orig.note: Greek: I have seen the Lord. Mary's words in John 20:18, in modern Greek editions.

carryVoice: Your line: she told them first. She was sent with the news, and she went. Rest well.
